text: I can bet all my chips! Yee-haw!"

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Then he's crestfallen when everybody folds. A normal player with some sophistication would think "I've got the nuts, I need to make something more on this hand. I'll bet $150, maybe the 3- to-l odds will induce a call. Better than nothing." But if this guy is just a beginner, why did he check on fourth street? After all, the deuce didn't make his straight (unless he had ace-trey, in which case his first two calls don't make much sense). If he has a straight, he had it on fourth street, where he checked. Was he planning to check-raise? That's not the mark of an excitable beginner who can't control himself. I'm thinking this betting pattern doesn't add up. Looks to me like there's a good chance this bet is just a pot- stealing bluff. You should seriously consider calling. One last thought. A world-class player is quite capable of shoving all his chips in the pot with a straight in a situation like this, hoping that his opponent will go through the same reasoning I just did and call. When you're up against someone really good, watch out, and take nothing for granted! Resolution: You call, and the small blind shows down A♥7♥. Your jacks win a $2,220 pot.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Let's make a couple of notes about our opponent's play. His bet on the end was a big mistake - a standard example of a no-win bet on the end. He had only top pair, and almost no one would call this bet in the face of the straight possibilities on the board unless they could at least beat top pair. But since he had top pair, there was no need to throw in all his chips to force you out. Top pair might be good enough to beat whatever you had, so he should have been happy to show the hand down. His hand was also good enough to make a play on the flop. At that point he had top pair (sevens) plus an ace plus four cards to a flush. He could reasonably think he had 14 outs twice (9 hearts, 3 aces, 2 sevens), which meant he was a slight favorite, plus a bet might win the pot right there. Checking was a mistake.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Situation: Early in a one-table satellite. The table is generally tight. Your hand: A♠Q♣ Action to you: Player A raises to $60. Players B, C, D, and E all fold. Pot now $105. Question: Do you call or raise? Answer: Call. At a tight table with a full complement of players, you need to assume that bets mean pretty much what they're supposed to mean. The guy in first position put in a raise under the gun, so he's supposed to have a good hand - a pair, or maybe ace-king or ace-queen.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: According to the Gap Concept, you need a hand at least as good as that to play. You've got it, but just barely, so you should play, but you shouldn't get that excited about your hand yet. It's a nice hand, but not a great one. In limit poker, you would frequently fold ace-queen in this position. At no-limit, position is far more important than at limit, since it carries the possibility of winning someone's entire stack, rather than just a couple of bets. Your good position lets you call here. Action: You call. The button and the small blind fold, and the big blind calls $30. The pot is now $195. Flop: T♠T♥9♣ Action: The big blind checks, and Player A bets $100. What's your play? Answer: Fold. Here's an example of the sandwich effect in action. You've missed the flop, but his bet of half the pot could be a standard continuation bet. If you were the only two players in the pot, a call could be justified. But now there's still another player to act behind you, and that's too much. Don't be seduced by the fact that the big blind only checked. Sure, he might be weak, but players who flop a set usually check as well.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: You can't assume a player is out of the pot until he's really out of it. Action: You actually call, and the big blind folds. The pot is now $395. Fourth Street: J♣ Action: Player A checks. You have an open-ended straight draw, and think you might be able to steal the pot. Should you try to steal, and if you say "yes, " should you bet $200 or go all-in for $540? Answer: You shouldn't try to steal here, but it's not a hopeless play. A better approach would be just to take a free card, and see if you can make a hand. So far you've committed only $160, and if you can get out of the hand without investing any more, you still have a shot (albeit not a great one) at the tournament. A steal attempt could end up in your being knocked out right here. If you really wanted to steal, you should probably put in $200 instead of $540. If your opponent has nothing, either bet should chase him away. If he raises you all-in after you bet $200, you can decide then what you want to do. Going all-in simply robs you of some flexibility with no real upside. Action: You in fact go all-in, and Player A calls. He turns over J♦J♠, and you're dead to his full house. His check on fourth street was just a trap.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: There's one more technical point to note about this hand. If you had bet $200, your opponent would have had a choice with his lock hand - put you all-in right away, or call and hope to get the last $340 out of you on fifth street. The latter play looks more clever and sophisticated, but it's actually just an elementary blunder. With the board showing jack-ten-nine and two clubs, he should assume that you have a draw at something, either a straight or a flush. If he goes all-in now, the draw possibility will force you to call. If he waits until fifth street, and you miss your draw (likely), you'll fold his bet. So with a lock hand and a draw showing, bet on fourth street to get all the chips.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Situation: Early in an online tournament. The big blind is a wild and aggressive player who likes to get in a pot and raise with anything. Player F seems solid and tight. Your hand: T♥T♣ Action to you: Players A and B fold. Question: Do you call or raise? Answer: You can't just call, because your hand is likely to be the best right now, but may well not be best if several players get in the pot, and the flop comes with a card or two higher than your tens. So you have to raise to cut down on the callers. I like to have a range of possible raises for a hand like this, so my opponents can't read the meaning of my bets easily. For this kind of situation, my range is three to five times the big blind. Within that range, I might vary my bets randomly, or I might let the situation govern my choice. Here you see that the player in the big blind is a wild and crazy guy to likes to play a lot of pots and raise aggressively. You shouldn't be afraid of driving him out with a good-sized bet, and you want as much of his money in the pot as you can get, so go to the high end of the range and raise to $100 here. Action: You actually raise to $60.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Players D and E fold, but the button (Player F) calls. The small blind folds and the big blind calls for another $40. The pot is now $190. Flop: 8♣7♠6♣ Action: The big blind checks. What do you do? Answer: That's a good but not great flop for you - three cards all lower than your pair, but with possible straight and flush draws out there. You should now bet something like three-fourths of the pot. If you get raised, be prepared to go all the way. Since you have two tens, it's unlikely you're facing someone with the high end of the straight, and it's very unlikely that anyone called before the flop with a five-four. Action: You bet $160. Player F calls, and the big blind folds. The pot is now $510. Fourth Street: T♦ Question: What do you do? Answer: You should bet a goodly amount here. If Player F has a nine, you're beaten, but he is unlikely to have one. He is a solid, tight player who probably would not call a raise with ace-nine or king-nine. In these small satellites and online tournaments, you have very little time to pile up

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: chips, so you have to press your good hands to the fullest. You can't worry much about the freak holdings that contain a nine. If you get raised, plan on calling. Action: You actually bet $200, and Player F calls. The pot is now $910. Fifth Street: 4♦ Question: What do you do? Answer: Now a straight draw on the other end! Yes, it's possible he's been calling all along and now you're dead. But you only have $490 left, and if you lose the tournament with your set of tens, so be it. This could be the best hand you see for quite awhile, and you should be prepared to go all the way with it. It's unlikely he's holding a four or a nine from the way the hand developed. Action: You go all-in for $490, and he calls, showing down a pair of aces. You win the pot. Mystery revealed - he was slowplaying aces all the way, and lost the hand on fourth street. It was a dangerous play, but worth doing very occasionally to keep your opponents guessing.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Situation: Early in a one-table satellite tournament. Player C is a wild man who plays most pots and likes to raise aggressively. Player G and the big blind seem solid. Your hand: J♠T♠ Action to you: Players A and B fold. Player C calls. Players D, E, and F fold. Player G calls. Pot is now $105. Question: What do you do? Answer: Since you're in the small blind, it costs you only $15 to call this bet. Despite your bad position on subsequent rounds, the 7-to-l pot odds make this a trivially easy call. Remember that you goal with suited connectors is to see a cheap flop. Here the flop is as cheap as it gets. One concern you should have is the presence of a really active player with a huge pile of chips. If he were still to act behind you, this is the sort of hand you might let go rather than play. But here he's already called, so you're free to act. Action: You call for $15 and the big blind checks. The pot is now $120. Flop: J♣3♠2♠ Question: You're first to act. What do you do? Answer: Short of flopping a straight or a flush, this is about as good as the flop can get for you. You've flopped top pair and a four-flush, and the two low cards help your flush while almost

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: certainly missing the other players. The question now is not whether to bet, but how much. You need to bet enough to make some money, but not so much as to drive people out. This is a hand where you don't mind callers, because of the flush possibility. I'd recommend a bet of about three-fourths of the pot, $80 to $90. Your only fears here are that you're up against a hand like queen-jack, or a very low pair that flopped trips. But right now those are long shots. Checking (with the idea of check-raising) is not a terrible play. Remember, however, that you need to bet your good hands frequently as part of a balanced strategy. You will be making bluffs and continuation bets, and these bets can't work unless balanced with legitimate bets. Action: You actually bet the pot, $130. The big blind calls, but the other two players fold. The pot is now $380. Fourth Street: K♥ Question: What now? Answer: The king didn't help you, but it may not have hurt you. Here's the problem, however, with bad position. You still have to lead here, and you're stepping into darkness. If you check, you'll still have to call a bet, and betting first gives you a chance to win the pot.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: I'd recommend a fourth-street continuation bet here, betting a little more than half the pot, something in the range of $150 to $220. With just a pair of jacks, you're not strong enough for a check-raise, so just make a straight value bet and see what happens. Action: You actually bet $50, and the big blind calls. The pot is now $480. Not a good choice of bet size. Remember that poker is first and foremost a game of information. Sometimes a larger bet is actually a defensive move, a way of protecting your whole stack, by sacrificing a few extra chips to get more information about the hand. Fifth Street: 5♣ Question: What's your play now? Answer: All you have now is second pair, and you've represented that from the beginning. So if you make a large bet, he'll call only if he can at least beat the second pair. On the other hand, if you make a small probing bet, you might head him off from making a bigger bet which you will be compelled to call. So your choices are checking or making a smallish bet. I like checking, but wouldn't argue with someone who wanted to lead out with a little bet. Action: You check, and he bets $200. Do you call or fold? Answer: You must call.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: The pot now has $680, and it costs you $200 to call, so you're getting 3.5-to-l on your money. If you were sure you were beaten, you could fold. But here you can't be sure, since he hasn't shown any strength until this last bet. Action: You call, and he shows A♠4♠, taking the pot with his low straight. So he was drawing to the nut flush, an inside straight, and an ace throughout. After the flop, he had 15 outs (9 spades, 3 fives - don't count the fives twice - and three aces), and he still had 15 outs on the last card. Both his calls were proper, as was his $200 bet on the end. It was just the right amount to get you to put some more money in because of the pot odds, and not so much as to chase you away. That's good poker. Be glad you didn't hit your flush, or you would have lost all your money!

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Situation: Early in a single-table online tournament. Your hand:4♠3♠ Action to you: Player A calls. Player B folds. Player C calls. Players D, E, and F all fold. Player G calls. Player H folds. The small blind folds. The pot is now $135. Question: Do you check or raise? Answer: This is a hand you would normally throw away, but you're delighted to see a free flop. Perhaps you'll get very lucky and flop a straight or a flush. You simply check. Action: You check. Pot remains $135. Flop: A♣2♣5♣ Question: You're first to act. What do you do? Answer: You've flopped a straight, but there are three flush cards on board. Some players are afraid to act in this situation, but you mustn't be. Remember, you've flopped a very strong hand. It's possible that you're already beaten. But it's much more likely that there are drawing hands out there that will beat you if you let them. If you don't bet, they'll bet at you and you'll have no idea where they stand. If someone has four clubs at this point, they're a 4-to-l underdog to make their flush on the turn. You need to make a big bet now to make sure they don't get those odds. Action: You are afraid to bet, and just check.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Players A and C check also. Now Player G bets $170. What do you do? Answer: You can call, of course, because you have a straight. Unfortunately, because you didn't lead out, you won't really know anything about Player G's hand. He might have a made flush. He might have a high club, and be trying to buy the pot now, with a fallback draw if anyone calls. He might have an ace. He might be stealing the pot when no one else bet. Now you have to learn something from the rest of the hand. A better play is to raise $350. If Player C, the big stack, goes all-in, you can throw your hand away. Otherwise, you'll do at least as well as by calling. If someone has two clubs, you will lose either way. If someone has one club, you will win instead of losing. And if no one has any clubs, you will make more money. Action: You call. Players A and C fold. The pot is now $475. Fourth Street: Q♥ Question: What do you do? Answer: You have to lead out. If he's still drawing to his flush, he's going to check behind you (if you check) and get a free draw. That's a disaster for you.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: If he hasn't made his flush yet, he's a 4-to-l underdog to get it on the last card, so bet enough to make a call by him incorrect. $200 is

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: plenty. Action: You don't bet, but check instead. He bets $200. What do you do? Answer: Raise him all-in. He's not acting like a guy who had the nuts on the flop. Instead of sucking money into the pot, he's trying to chase people out with big bets. Think about it. Is this how you would play a lock hand? Also remember that a straight is a very strong hand. You're still probably best here, so make him pay. Action: You fold. He scoops up the pot without showing his hand. You made three big blunders. You didn't lead out with a very strong hand, so you didn't know where you stood when he bet. Then you repeated that mistake. Then you folded what was probably the winning hand. All of this might well have been avoided with a bet on the flop. Remember that leading out with a bet buys you information and cuts down on your volatility by forcing your opponents to reveal their strength. Check-raising, on the other hand, buys you more information at a higher price and increases your volatility.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Situation: Middle of an online tournament Your hand: Q♠T♣ Action to you: Players A and B fold. Player C calls for $60. Player D folds. Player E calls. Player F calls. The small blind calls for an additional $30. The pot is now $300. Question: Do you check or raise? Answer: You're quite happy to check. You're in bad position, and you don't have that much of a hand. So seeing a free flop is great. Action: You check. Flop: T♠9♠2♦ Action: The small blind bets $130. The pot is $430. What do you do? Answer: You've caught top pair, with a decent kicker. If the small blind had checked, you should have led out for about two-thirds of the pot, say about $200. The small blind's bet puts you in a much tougher position. You're caught in a sandwich, and there's no good way out. You don't want to let the players behind you in so cheaply, since they're easily getting the odds to call with a drawing hand. But you don't really want to raise a lot here - you don't know where you stand, and there are a lot of active players. While it's not a happy play, here the best risk-reward ratio might just be a passive call.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Action: You call for $130. Player C calls. Player E folds. Player F calls. The pot is now $820. Fourth Street: T♦ Action: The small blind checks. What do you do? Answer: You have trip tens. The board now shows two spades and two diamonds, so there are plenty of draws available. You probably have the best hand now, but deciding how much to bet is a problem. You've got two competing goals: betting a small enough amount to get people to call, but a large enough amount to get the drawers to fold. Right now the pot is big enough so that getting lots of new money in is not as high a priority as winning the money that's already out there. You should bet about three-fourths of the pot, about $600. Anyone drawing to a flush won't be getting the right odds to call. (They'll need 4-to-l, and they'll be getting only a little over 2-to-l.) If anyone else wants to call that bet, well that's fine. Note that there's no need to go all-in, because such a bet is more likely to chase away the weaker hands that you want to stick around. Action: You actually bet only $320. Player C folds. Player F calls. The small blind calls. The pot is now $1,780.

author: Dan Harrington
chapter: 4. Fifth street is the K♦. Should you bet?
source_file: Harrington_on_Hold_em_Expert_Strategy_fo.pdf
text: Fifth Street: A♠ Action: The small blind goes all-in for $1,310. What do you do? Answer: Cry because you bet too little last turn. Notice what happened. The pot was $820, you bet $320, then Player F put in $320, making the pot $1,460. The small blind now had to put in $320 for a shot at a pot of $ 1,460, meaning that he had better than the 4-to-l odds he needed if he was drawing at a flush. And then the flush card hit. You have to fold here. He's been representing a flush draw all along, and the third spade came, and now his bet says he has it. More important, he's going all-in against two players, not just one, so it's unlikely he's running a bluff. If I had to guess, he's probably been playing something like K♠J♠, with the flush draw and two overcards to the board. It's tough to fold trips, but be glad you've at least kept some chips. Resolution: You fold, and Player F folds.

author: Dan Harrington

text: Conclusion We've covered a lot of ground in Volume I. Even if you've never played in a major event, you should now have a good idea of the kinds of things that good no-limit hold ’em players are thinking about as they work their way through a tournament. There are three main ideas that you should take away from this book: 1. No-limit hold ’em is a very complex game. It's not all about running outrageous bluffs or interpreting your opponent's facial ticks (although both will happen from time to time). Instead it's a game of memory, position, calculation, alertness, and patience, where you need to constantly reorient yourself with respect to your position at the table, the changing stack and blind sizes, the demonstrated habits of your opponents, and the actual strength of your cards. 2. Pot odds are paramount. Like all gamblers and investors, a no-limit hold ’em player is constantly trying to make good bets at favorable odds. Without knowing the pot odds, you can't even make an educated guess as to the wisdom of shoving your chips into this particular pot. Calculating pot odds must be automatic and routine. 3.

text: mostly reflects a conservative style of play, partly because that's how I play and partly because that's the easiest style to learn if you're a newcomer. But remember that it's not the only way to play poker. With the basics of no-limit hold ’em strategy now covered, I'll move on in Volume II to more advanced topics. Here's a quick preview. Making moves. In Volume II focused mostly on what are called value bets, where you bet either because you believe you have the best hand and want to get more money in the pot, or because you might have the best hand and think the pot odds justify playing. But there's another whole category of plays called moves, where you hope to win the pot (or a much bigger pot) by fundamentally misrepresenting the value of your hand. In this section we'll look at the types of moves available and the preconditions for making certain moves successful. Inflection points. When your stack is large relative to the blinds and antes, you're free to play more or less as you wish. As the blinds and antes increase relative to your stack, your approach must change. I call the places where your strategy changes inflection points.

text: “A small leak will sink a great ship.” -Benjamin Franklin (The guy on $100 bills) Every time you buy into the poker table and hand over some Benjamins for some red chips imagine Uncle Benny giving you that parting advice. If you listen, when you come back in a few hours you should be getting Uncle Benny, some of his twins and a few dead presidents back. When you cash out, the chips you win are not different than the chips you fail to lose. Many players know how to win in good situations, but they don’t know how to not lose in bad situations. All of us at Red Chip Poker have coached players that have leaks in their game. Those leaks can cost $30 or more an hour. Handicapping yourself with costly errors will turn any winning player into a losing one. Plugging those leaks can turn losing players into winning players. This book is about ten things that poker players should stop doing. It is not just a “Fold pre-flop” book. We cover hand selection, bad bet sizing and the tilt monster. This is a simple book. There is a lot more depth in our other material.

book_title: STOP: 10 Things Good Poker Players Don't Do
author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: Find it at: RedChipPoker.com TOP TILTING BY SWEENEY “Tilt is anything that takes you off your A-game — it could be a situation, a thought, an emotional reaction or a myriad of other things.” – Dr. Tricia Cardner We’ve all experienced tilt in one form or another. Humans are emotional by nature and those emotions flare up regularly on the table. Maybe somebody on the table is bullying you and you have an emotional response to that. Maybe somebody just sucked out on you. Maybe you just won $500 in an hour and you have an emotional response to that. These are common actions and reactions on any poker table. But tilt is something we want to avoid at all costs. In an ideal world we would be ice-cold robots when we are playing poker. All decisions being calculated, optimized, and without emotion. Alas, we are not robots, and

book_title: STOP: 10 Things Good Poker Players Don't Do
author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: thus we have to understand tilt at a deeper level to ensure it doesn’t creep up in our game and result in us losing extra money. First, let’s explore the three most common forms of tilt: LOSING TILT This is the most common form of tilt. A player loses a big pot after getting sucked out, angrily rebuys, and then loses another stack within a few minutes playing recklessly. Chances are you’ve done this as well (I know I sure have). It’s extremely important that we are able to identify when someone is experiencing this form of tilt so we can put ourselves in a position to capture the money they want to throw away. And it’s also important that we eliminate this kind of tilt from our own game. WINNER ’S TILT The opposite of Losing Tilt is Winner’s Tilt. This is when a player is winning and then immediately changes their game. One form of Winner’s Tilt is leaving a good game early in an effort to “lock-up a win” due to the fear of giving any of their winnings back. Another form is playing much looser since “who cares? I’m already up so much money anyway!” Both are suboptimal reactions and take us out of our A-game.

book_title: STOP: 10 Things Good Poker Players Don't Do
author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: BOREDOM TILT Have you ever seen the player who has done nothing but fold for two hours and then randomly, out of the blue, he decides to make some absurd play? Their absurd play is almost always a reaction to Boredom Tilt. Most of us have fallen prey to this at one time or another; either playing a bad hand just because we are bored to want to see a flop or refusing to fold a second-best hand post-flop because it’s been forever since we’ve gotten a good starting hand. All forms of tilt take us away from our A-game and degrade our edge on the table. And the severity of tilt can range from losing a couple extra dollars in a hand to losing multiple stacks in an orbit. For what it’s worth, if you tilt and spew $200 for no reason, it’s going to take you a long time to recoup that loss. Even if you are crushing the game for $20/hr, it will take you 10 hours at an expected win rate to get that back. And if you are only winning at $8/hr, it will take you 25 hours at an expected win rate to win it back!

book_title: STOP: 10 Things Good Poker Players Don't Do
author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: You already know tilt is bad, and you already know tilt is costing you money. But how can you stop tilting? Here are three ways to conquer tilt: UNDERSTAND YOUR TRIGGERS First, you need to understand your “tilt triggers”...those actions that happen that initiate your tilt. Once you know what your triggers are, it becomes easier to either stop tilt dead in its tracks...or to recognize it’s time to take a step away from the table. The next time you begin to tilt, start asking yourself a series of internal questions so that you can identify the core of the issue. A conversation may look like this: “Why did I just four bet shove with AJ against a nit?” I was angry that I got sucked out on by a 2-outter the hand before. “Why did getting 2-outted affect me so much?” Because I needed to win that pot to get back to break-even on the session. “Can you control that you get 2-outted?” No. “Is there any sense getting mad about something you can’t control?” No. “If you get 2-outted again, could you be OK with it so long as you got your money in with an edge?” Yes. The trigger here was getting two-outted (a common thing that players get upset about), and the response was spewing off a stack.

book_title: STOP: 10 Things Good Poker Players Don't Do
author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: But if we ask ourselves some simple and logical questions we see what created the negative action and why we did it. Pro tip: If the answer to that last question was ‘No’, this player should make it a habit to take a five minute walk anytime they get two-outted rather than stay at the table and make really bad decisions BREATHE This may seem obvious, but it’s vital when we begin to feel those tilting waves sweeping over us. Rather than succumb to the tilt, take a few deep breaths (a few seconds on the inhale, a moment to hold it, and a few seconds

book_title: STOP: 10 Things Good Poker Players Don't Do
author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: to exhale). Deep breathing is one of the easiest ways to reset yourself and avoid letting tilt take over you. Seriously, the next time you begin to feel tilt creeping in, take five deep breaths and see how you feel. If you still feel tilty after those deep breaths, take a few minutes away from the table and return to play once you feel tilt- free again. PAUSE FIRST . REVIEW LATER Starting to feel tilty? Pause and take a moment. Begin breathing, begin trying to identify the trigger, and see if the severity of this tilt is going to cost you any money. The more severe the tilt, the more quickly you should just step away from the table and walk for a few minutes to clear your head. Understanding tilt in real-time is vital to ensuring you don’t get taken off your A-game, but reviewing tilt and building emotion control away from the table is vital to long-term success. The day after every session you should sit down and ask yourself questions like “Did I tilt at all during my session yesterday?” If the answer is yes, write down what tilted you, how you reacted when you tilted, and what you could do to avoid tilting in the future.

author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: This exercise is great not just for poker, but for real-life. If you find yourself tilting while driving (road rage), or getting tilty when someone disagrees with you...explore the situation later and understand yourself at deeper level. The better you understand yourself, your triggers, and your common reactions; the easier it is to work on them and eventually erase them. It’s not easy to have pure emotional control, but the pursuit of it is crucial to your success on the felt. To quote Christian Soto: “Poker is a game of decisions. Whoever makes the most correct decisions wins. Nothing else matters, not even the money” Notice nothing in there mentions emotions or ego. Poker is a game of decision making and tilt just keeps you from making the best decisions you can. So get a handle on your tilt so you can keep a better handle on your bankroll...and take bankrolls from your tilting opponents! BOTTOM LINE : 1. Tilt happens, but it costs you a ton of money. Learn how and why you tilt

Your tilt only costs you money. It never helps you in the long run TOP OPEN-LIMPING BY HULL A Novice was limping whenever he had a slightly reasonable hand and then folding when he missed or was raised. The Master spoke sternly: “You cannot win by limping into pots only hoping to get lucky.” The Master sat down and limped into a pot. The novice was enlightened. If the only way you can win a pot is by making a hand, you cannot win at Hold’em. It is tough to make a pair in Hold’em, it is even harder to make a pair that you like. Believe it or not, limping and open limping is an advanced maneuver, which is beyond the scope of this book. When you have progressed to the point that you can identify why and where limping fits into your aggressive winning style, then you too will be able to add limping back into your arsenal. Until then, the only unraised pots you should be in are those where you are in the Big Blind and check your option. Try this for three sessions: do not limp into any pots. What are the exceptions?

text: None, there are no exceptions. You cannot be the first limper. You cannot limp behind a limper. No limping. Seriously, none. You may call a raise and play poker. Just make sure you think about three- betting and think about folding before you call. If no one has entered the pot yet and you wish to play, raise. Make is a solid raise to 5x or 6x. (Remember we are talking about live poker here, so this is actually normal and considered reasonable.) If someone else has limped into the pot and you want to play, make it an even bigger raise. At a $1-$2 game, with one limper, make it $15. Two or three limpers? Make it $20 or $22. Four limpers? Fire it up to $25.

author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney

text: Why so big? Isn’t $7 more reasonable? We bet or raise to capitalize on our opponents’ mistakes and cause them to make bigger mistakes later. The vast majority of opponents will limp into pots with wide and weak ranges. We can punish that mistake with a healthy raise to $15 or more. We will pick up a lot of pots uncontested. These small pots add up. I routinely rack out of $1-$2 games with $80 in white chips. These are all from small pots that I raise and pick-up preflop If we only make it $7, the limpers are likely to make another $5 mistake by calling. The problem is, this second mistake is harder to capitalize on. One limp-caller encourages the next. The tools of aggression we have do not work as well in bloated, multi-way pots. In this situation, the only way left to win is to make a hand. Although our range is stronger than the limp-callers — so we will win more than our share of these hands — we can do better. When, instead, we make a large raise pre-flop, we take the Villains out of their comfort zone. They mostly just fold to us. The Villains fold often enough that this move might possibly make us money immediately, even with blank cards. We don’t have blank cards though.

author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney

text: Furthermore, we are usually going to only face one Villain instead of four. Both of these things help us. Now we have a variety of strategies to use, and the solo Villain is ready to commit the second mistake of the limp-caller: Fit or fold on the flop. Not limping into pots will encourage you to play tighter and to play more aggressive. Your image will change. People will get sick of you. They will grumble, complain, caterwaul, bleat, squawk, and whimper. They will call you, “Sir Raise-a-lot.” They will mumble, “There he goes again.” They will mutter, “This is just a $2 hand.” They will murmur about, “Waiting for a better spot.” What they won’t do is play back at you without a hand. The more they complain the better. Complaining means their only defense is to try and shame you into playing in a way that makes them more comfortable. You know you have the right strategy when you hear these empty threats and protestations.

text: What do you need to worry about? That quiet guy. The one that took a seat change button after your third raise. He will find his way to your immediate left. We already know why he is moving and what he is thinking about. He is coming after you, but the rest of this book will help you deal with him. BOTTOM LINE : 1. Don’t limp for three sessions. 2. Raise bigger pre-flop. 3. Consider re-raising or folding before you call a raise. 4. Want to limp, see Rule One. 5. Seriously, see Rule One. TOP PLAYING IN BAD SPOTS BY SOTO No one drives to the local card room to fold. Folding is boring. We love action. However, a common mistake is playing too wide of a range in bad situations. As we improve, we slowly gather the license to play more hands. The reason elite players can play a wider array of hands is because they have the weapons in their arsenal to dig themselves out of marginal situations. Until we have the same post-flop skill edge, we should avoid marginal spots and always avoid bad spots. It pains me to say this, but tight can be correct in a lot of situations as we are honing our postflop skills.

book_title: STOP: 10 Things Good Poker Players Don't Do
author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: The reason tight can work when we are starting this journey is because if we are playing tighter, the range we have at the flop will have higher equity as a whole. This will make our decisions easier going forward. Playing a solid range can keep you away from marginal situations where you will have the potential to make errors. Of course, playing a tight range overall can leave expected value on the table. With time we can learn to pick that up too. In other portions of this book, there will be chapters concerning limping and what hands we choose to include in our pre-flop opening raise range. As a result, I will not touch on these subjects in this chapter. I will, however, discuss cold-calling an open-raise and the decision matrix that goes into that. (Cold-calling is calling a bet or re-raise without having put any money into the pot before that call.)

book_title: STOP: 10 Things Good Poker Players Don't Do
author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: It may be fairly common for us to see a player win a big pot with J-To after calling an open from middle position, flopping an open ended draw, getting there, and beating another strong hand for a big pot. It may be tempting to do the same. However, this may have been a long term losing play. I can almost assure you this call pre-flop will be a losing one long term. Hands that we are looking to cold-call will include high equity hands that play well versus the range of hands our opponent chooses to open. For example, these hands may include hands such as 6-6 — T-T, 7-8s — K-Qs, A-Ts+, A-Qo. Depending on stack depths we may choose to include small pocket pairs in our range in order to set-mine. A rule of thumb you may want to use when first determining whether or not to cold-call with small pairs or suited connectors is only do so if both you and your opponent has 20 times the open raise behind. For example, if your opponent opens to $12, we should both have $240 behind before you call. This rule can be broken for numerous reasons, including sources of implied odds, opponents being especially weak post- flop, or many other reasons.

text: However, this is a good starting point in determining if the situation is profitable. To direct you towards a hand chart of a coldcall range would be unfair and may box you in as you move forward. Therefore, I will not do that. I will, however, say that the range above is a good starting point. If you want to go outside the constraints of that range then you will need to have extended list of reasons to do so. There are a lot of hands that are not included in the range above that you might usually consider playing. For example, what do we do with hands like K-Jo or hands like A-To? Shifting these hands towards a three-bet bluff range will allow you to win the pot more often than you will by coldcalling. This will also avoid you being in difficult multi-way pots with hands that are sometimes dominated by another player’s hole cards. In war, battles are won and lost in the trenches. Cash game poker is no different. Unlike tournaments, most of the play in cash games is post-flop. Therefore, we should bring a set of weapons that will allow us to win. We need to be brutally honest in regards to our abilities.

The game is fluid, and it is important to stay on top of it TOP LEADING WEAK PAIRS BY MILLER Here’s the situation. You’ve got a pair you aren’t sure about. It might be top pair but with a fishy kicker like a six or a nine. Or maybe it’s a pocket pair below top pair like T-T on a Q-high board. Or perhaps it’s middle pair like A-8 on a J-8-3 flop. Your opponent bet the flop, and you called with your pair. You know your opponent easily could have a better pair than yours, in which case you likely shouldn’t continue past the turn. On the other hand, your opponent could just be stabbing at the pot, and your pair could be best. With these medium- strength pairs, you’re always in doubt. So what do you do? If you’re like a lot of small stakes players, you try to “see where you’re at” with a weak lead.

text: Most small stakes players use this play, but by the end of the chapter you’ll see why you should not. What’s a weak lead? It’s when you interrupt the betting sequence with a particularly small bet. So say you’re playing $1-$3. Your opponent openraises to $12, and three people call, including you in the big blind. You have 8-8. There’s $49 in the pot and four players. The flop comes T-4-3. You check, and the preflop raiser bets $20. The other two players fold, and you call. There’s $89 in the pot. The turn comes a 6. You bet out. How much? You try $25. Or maybe $30. Or maybe $35. But not $60, and definitely not $80. That’s a weak lead. You check-call the flop but then bet out on the turn, and you choose a bet size that’s fairly small compared to the previous bet and the pot size.

You might check, hoping to get a check-raise in. Or, if you’re worried your opponent will check behind, you’ll bet out. But you won’t bet $25 or $30. You’ll bet $50 or $60 or $80. Because if you make the nuts, you want to get some money into the pot. Let’s go back to the hand where you have 8-8. Because, let’s be honest, you’re going to have that pair way more often than you’ll have the nuts. You bet out for $30. Your opponent raises you to $100. What do you do ? At this point, the only sensible thing to do is fold. You were worried about the strength of your pair, and your opponent is telling you clearly that it’s no good. With 8-8 you have only two outs to improve, and there’s a decent chance it will cost you a stack to find out if he’s bluffing. But let’s back it up. You should not bet the turn in the first place. text: Throw the weak lead into the trash can of bad no-limit hold’em plays. Why? Information. People who use the weak lead think they are doing it to gather information. They’re trying to see where they’re at. The problem is that they’re giving away more valuable information than they’re getting in return. If I bet the flop and you call out of the blind, I think there’s a good chance you have a weak pair (since those hands are so common). There’s also a chance you are calling with a draw or with a big hand like a set. I can’t define your hand beyond that. Probably a pair, but maybe a draw and maybe something big. The moment you bet the turn, you snap that picture into high def clarity. If you bet $20 or $30 or $35, I know you’ve got the pair. If you bet $50 or $60 or $80, I know you probably hit your hand hard. I can use that information to maximal advantage. If you bet big, I just fold. If you bet small, I take it as a

text: If you see someone else make this play, raise! You know how some players will tell you, “I’ll fold if you raise?” Well, this weak lead play tells you the same thing non-verbally. When someone bets out like this, they’re saying they plan to fold if you raise. So do it TOP PAYING THEM OFF BY MILLER This concept is simple but powerful. It’s based on a strategic idea that applies nearly universally in small stakes no-limit hold’em games. When people make big bets and raises on the turn and river, they aren’t bluffing. It’s not that they never bluff. But there is a theoretical percentage of the time that players should be bluffing if they want to play well. In nearly all cases, small stakes players will fall short of this theoretical percentage with their bluffing when the big bets come out. They bluff— but they don’t bluff often enough to make you want to call.

text: Therefore, if someone makes a big bet or raise, you should assume they have the hand they are representing. This usually means you should fold. If you should fold, you should fold. Every time. That’s the hard part. It’s easy to talk yourself into calling. Maybe you feel like you’re being bullied, so you decide you’re going to take a stand. (At $1-$2, it’s more likely you’re just running bad than that your opponent is intentionally manipulating you.) Maybe you flopped a big hand, and you just can’t accept that you were outdrawn. Maybe it’s not clear what your opponent is representing, and you are confused or curious. I don’t care. Fold. Learning to fold in these situations is one of the skills most critical to beating $1-$2 games. Here’s an example. It’s a $1-$2 game. You have A-K. Two players limp, and you make it $12 to go. The river is the 2 . Your opponent says, “Same bet,” and throws out $20 more. This is something you’ll see opponents do from time to time. You may be prone to do it too. If so, stop. It’s not good. There are a few problems with this sort of play. First is that, like the weak lead from an earlier chapter, this play divulges way too much information about your hand. Players don’t call the “same bet” when they have the nuts. It’s usually a weak or moderate pair—just the sort of hand people like to use the weak lead play with. So when your opponents say, “same bet,” they might as well be saying, “I’ll fold if you raise.” It’s a little less reliable of a message with the same bettors as with the weak leaders, but it’s reliable enough to use it as a green light to bluff Beyond divulging information about their hand, players who use this “same bet” line also typically telegraph their intentions on a future betting round.

text: If you hear someone say, “same bet” on the turn and you call, it’s highly likely your opponent will also make the same bet on the river, regardless of what comes. No-limit hold’em is a game of information hiding. You want to hide as much information as possible about your cards from your opponents. But you also want to hide information about your future intentions from your opponents. If you bet the turn and your opponent calls, you want there to be doubt about whether you will check the river or whether you will bet the river and, if so, how much. The players who make take the “same bet” line remove most of this doubt about the future because you can expect a bet, and you can expect it to be the same size as the flop and turn bets. Why is this important? First, you can safely delay a raise until the river if you can reliably assume your opponent will keep betting. This allows you to deny more information

If your opponent were less predictable, you might feel the need to raise earlier with strong hands. Second, you know, in advance, the price to draw to a hand. So say you flop a weak draw like a gutshot. If your opponent bets the flop, you may be unsure whether you will be getting the right price to call. Part of the problem is you aren’t sure how much it will cost on the turn. So if you call now and miss, you might get blown off your hand on the turn. However, if your opponent launches a “same bet” sort of betting line, you can fairly accurately price out your draw on both the turn and river and make more profitable decisions. Another reason to avoid the “same bet” idea is that it simply doesn’t get value for your hands. As I mentioned in the last chapter, one of the best ways to gain a persistent advantage is by refusing to pay off your opponents’ good hands while they pay off yours. But in order to make this a real advantage, you have to get them to pay. You have to put stacks in play.

When you stick to little bets, you limit your upside, and you also limit the total advantage you can generate for yourself. The same logic applies to betting lines that are small and predictable. Instead of $20-$20-$20, small and predictable. Instead of $20-$20-$20, $20-$25. Any betting line you use regularly that includes a series of small, predictably sized bets falls into this category. Every once in a while it can be good to use a betting series like this, but if you do so regularly and predictably, stop. Instead, just make bigger bets. Put stacks in play. Bet $20 and then $50 and then $150. Betsizing is a complex topic, but in general you’ll be a much more dangerous opponent if you are getting the chips out of your stack and onto the felt. Three-bet ranges are almost exclusively strong-side weighted towards Q- Q+/A-K. This can be fine when you are playing against opponents who do not pay attention or are too weak to care about anything except the cards in front of them. However, when you face a more competent group of opponents or ones who are still weak but pay just enough attention to notice your tendencies, you will need to find alternative ways to win three-bet pots without just having the goods. Which way our opponents react to three-bets will determine how we construct the range to three-bet. If our opponents are the type to either fold or four-bet when facing three-bet, then we want to construct a polarized three bet range.

text: This will consist of hands that have a fairly easy decision tree when facing a four-bet. For example, a typical polarized three-bet range will consist of Q-Q+/A-K for value and A-2s — A-5s/Weak K-Xs for bluffs. The reason why it is constructed in this fashion is because when facing a four-bet the bluff portion of your range has an easy decision; we fold, unless we have some reason to believe our opponent is four-bet bluffing and will fold to a five-bet The reason some polarized three-bet ranges contain A-X/K-X type hands for bluffs is because they contain a blocker. A blocker in this sense is that given we hold an Ace or King in our hand, it makes it less likely that our opponents hold some of the strongest hands in their range. To illustrate this I’ll give you an example. There are 16 combinations of Ace-King available preflop. However, if we hold an Ace in our hand we have now removed it from possibly being in our opponent’s hand. Therefore, now there are only 12 combinations of A-K. That’s a 25% decrease. As a result, this increases the probability of our opponents folding.

text: When our opponents are the type to want to see many flops, our strategy will be forced to shift. We will need higher equity hands, assuming we will be going to the flop at a higher frequency. This is a good time to use a depolarized three-bet range. A common depolarized three-bet range will be constructed in such a way to include 9-9+/K-Jo+/ A-To+.This range is called depolarized because it has strong, weak, and medium strength hands in it. In contrast, a polarized range has only weak and strong hands. A depolarized range will be easier to play post-flop when we do get called. We should be able to get value for our hand those times that we do make a hand. This value extraction will require excellent hand reading and post-flop play Who or when we choose to three-bet bluff will be based on our opponent’s frequency. text: 2. When choosing how to construct our three-bet range, take into account how our opponent combats three-bets. Pending their likely action, we will choose a range our accordingly. 3. Do not bail out poor post-flop players by them three-betting pre-flop. TOP SLOWPLAYING BY SWEENEY There are only two absolutes in poker: 1. Never fold A-A pre-flop in a NLHE cash game 2. Never fold a royal flush Every other rule has some wiggle-room. And the same thing is true for slowplaying. It’s not to say that slowplaying is never correct; rather slowplaying is something players do far too often. Slowplaying is when we play a strong hand very slowly. When we just call a flop and turn bet with a set. When we check all three streets with the nut straight. When we take a seemingly tricky and passive line with A-A. All of these are examples of slowplaying. And all of these are things I’d prefer you don’t do again. Let’s take a common example at $1/$2. You raise to $10 pre-flop with 7-7, get two callers, and the flop is: K -7 -3 You check, one player bets $15, one player calls $15, and then you call. In this example, we had two different opportunities to be aggressive.

author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
chapter: 1. Never fold A-A pre-flop in a NLHE cash game
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: We could have continuation bet with our set. Or, if we did decide to check, we could have check-raised. The issue with slowplaying here is threefold: 1. We are keeping the pot very small 2. We raise a red flag when we get aggressive later in the hand 3. We take some hands out of our aggressive range If all of us started the hand with $300, the pot will be $75 after we call and we’ll all have $275 left. It’s possible to get all-in at some point in the hand, but will it happen that often? Probably not. Primarily because of point two. If we check-call the flop and then check-raise the turn, is anyone going to be fooled and give us tons of action with their K-T? If we check-call the flop and check-call the turn, is anyone going to call our shove on the river?

author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney
chapter: 1. Never fold A-A pre-flop in a NLHE cash game
source_file: STOP 10 Things Good Poker Players Dont Do (Red Chip Poker, Ed Miller, James Sweeney etc.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: Most likely not because that line looks insanely strong. Even unsophisticated players know to be scared when a slowplayer gets aggressive on the turn or river. So by slowplaying we end up leaving a heap of value on the table and miss the chance of stacking someone. The last point is also very important. If we would check and slowplay with sets on this board, what hands are we betting? By checking these hands our betting range becomes weaker and weaker, when in reality we want to be betting the flop a large percentage of the time. This point becomes even more important when you play against stronger players. Rather than slowplay here, we should bet out. It’s much easier to get an opponent to call three bets with K-X than it is to get them to stack off when we check-call the flop and check-raise the turn. It’s much easier to grow a pot when we bet, rather than check and risk everyone checking as well. And it’s much easier to ensure our betting range is solid when we bet with our strongest hands. This isn’t to say that we should never slowplay though.

author: Ed Miller & James Sweeney

text: There are situations where a player has a bluff such a large percentage of the time that it’s fruitful for us to just check and let them bluff their stack off. There are times when we could checkraise an opponent and induce more mistakes from them than by just betting the turn ourself. But players trick themselves into thinking these rare occurrences are more common than they actually are. For your next three sessions I challenge you to not slowplay even once. That means you always re-raise your Aces and Kings pre-flop. That means you always continuation bet your big hands (even things like top set). And that means you always continue betting when you hit a draw. Notice the kinds of action you get and don’t be surprised when you see someone call you down all three streets with nothing but a weak top-pair. BOTTOM -LINE : 1. When in doubt, keep being aggressive and keep betting. 2. Slowplaying can be the right play, but it’s usually not. 3. Avoid slowplaying so you can keep control of the hand, so you can control the size of the bets, and so you can take advantage of players who simply call with too many weak hands

text: TOP PLAYING BAD HANDS BY SWEENEY Playing the wrong hands against bad players will leave some money on the table. Playing the wrong hands against decent players will leave you in the negative. Playing the wrong hands against great players will get you destroyed. Hand selection is a key component to making money in poker. But truth be told, I dislike starting hand charts. They are over-simplified, they are incomplete, and they change over time. That being said, I still always look for a starting hand chart when learning a new game so I have some sort of baseline for playing hands. So I’m going to share my starting hand chart for $1/$2 live cash games but with some clear caveats: 1. These charts show what you should openraise with in a $1/$2 cash game. They do not discuss open-limping, calling raises, raising over a number of limpers, or anything else. 2. These charts assume you have $200 or more in front of you and that the average person at your table has at least $200. 3. These charts are a starting point. When certain dynamics are present these ranges could be much tighter or much looser. 4. Your edge in the game will influence the exact range of hands you play.

text: If you are running over the table, you may be able to add in more hands. First, let’s remember the power of position. When it folds to us on the button, there are only two players to contend with when fighting for the blinds. But when we are first to act pre-flop, there are up to nine players between ourselves and the blinds. Plus, when we raise from any position between UTG and the CO we stand a chance to get action and be out of position when we go postflop. All this means we want to play many more hands from late position and far fewer hands from early position. Let’s start by discussing which hands we should open from early position. When we get an opportunity to open-raise from early position, this is the range I suggest you use :

Notice we aren’t even open-raising seemingly strong hands like A-J, J-Ts, or anything else. And since you aren’t going to open- limp anymore (you read that chapter already, right?), this means you know exactly which hands to play when you are first to enter the pot in a $1/$2 game. text: Button Open-Raise Range: 30% Of Hands Notice that as a default we are raising three times as many hands from the button as we are from early position. This again is due to the number of players left to contend with before we can pick up the blinds (and yes, fighting for those $3 is 100% worthwhile and adds up in the long run). But our ranges from late position, and in many situations middle position as well, are very flexible. Meaning a rigid starting hand chart can force us to miss many prime opportunities. Here are two clear examples where we would want to deviate from these charts. First, Q-Js is on the open-raise chart from middle position. But on this particular table the players left to act are super aggressive. They are three betting and four betting often, and the chances of getting just a single caller is extremely low. On this table, it doesn’t make sense to openraise since we are going to get three bet often and will be forced to fold a ton of the time. So rather than open-raise and fold when you face an inevitable three-bet... you should not open-raise and rather just fold instead. In this dynamic, you can use this same logic with hands like 9-8s, 4-4, and 2-2 as well.

text: Second, A-8o is not on the open-raise chart from the hijack (HJ). But on this particular table the players left to act are very tight. You anticipate everyone will fold a large percentage of the time if you open-raise to $10, and if they don’t fold pre-flop, they aren’t going to fight very hard post-flop. This is a prime spot to open-raise more hands than the chart suggests since you will find yourself in many profitable spots when you open, and the same logic carries over to things like Q-9o, 7-5s, etc. BOTTOM LINE : 1. Tight is right from early position. But as you get closer to the button, you should be opening more and more hands. Similarly, you should be more selective when you (or many of the players at the table) have stacks of $100 or less. 2. Consider the exact dynamic and players at your table. When the table is tighter, open more hands. When the table is looser, be more selective, especially when they are three-betting quite often

He has recently invented a new game called Poker Challenge, soon to appear in casinos. David attributes his standing in the gambling community to three things: I.The fact that he presents his ideas as simply as possible (sometimes with Mason Malmuth and/or Ed Miller) even though these ideas frequently involve concepts that are deep, subtle, and not to be found elsewhere. 2.The fact that the things he says and writes can be counted on to be accurate. 3.The fact that to this day a large portion of his income is still derived from gambling (usually poker but occasionally blackjack, sports betting, horses, video games, casino promotions, or casino tournaments).

text: Preface This book is about the general theories and concepts of poker play, which are operative in nearly every variation of poker from five-card draw to Texas hold 'em. It is not a how-to book in the sense of providing the basic rules and a step-by-step procedure for playing the various games. Beginning poker players sometimes ask, "What do you do in this particular situation?" There is really no correct answer to that question because it's the wrong question. Rules of thumb that say to fold one hand, call with another, and raise with yet another simply won't get a poker player beyond the beginning stages. The right question is: "What do you consider in this particular situation before determining what to do?" The Theory of Poker addresses itself to such considerations. It analyzes every aspect of a poker hand from the ante structure to play after the last card has been dealt. By explaining the logic of poker, the book will, I hope, show the reader what kinds of things to think about in order to become a better player. To illustrate the concepts presented, I use primarily five games - five-card draw, seven-card stud, hold 'em, draw lowball, and razz or seven-card lowball.

author: David Sklansky
source_file: The Theory of Poker A Professional Poker Player Teaches You How To Think Like One (David Sklansky) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text: Chapter One Beyond Beginning Poker The beauty of poker is that on the surface it is a game of utter simplicity, yet beneath the surface it is profound, rich, and full of subtlety. Because its basic rules are so simple, anyone can learn poker in a few minutes, and novice players may even think they're pretty good after a few hours. From the expert's point of view, the veneer of simplicity that deludes so many players into thinking they're good is the profitable side of the game's beauty. It doesn't take long for pool players or golfers to realize they're outclassed and to demand that a match be handicapped, but losers in poker return to the table over and over again, donating their money and blaming their losses on bad luck, not bad play. It's true that in any given session the best of players can get unlucky. Going into the final day ofthe 1981 world championship of poker, Bobby Baldwin of Tulsa, Oklahoma, had a substantial lead over the eight other surviving players. Within a couple of hours he had two hands beat when his opponents outdrew him on the final card on 21-to-1 shots. Suddenly he was out of the tournament.
